concepts.name: De-industrialization Thesis: Nature and Debate
key_dimensions: Definition and core argument by nationalist historians (Dadabhai Naoroji, R.C. Dutt)
Counter-arguments by Cambridge School historians (Morris D. Morris) questioning the extent of de-industrialization
Distinction between absolute de-industrialization vs. relative de-industrialization
Statistical evidence and methodological disputes around occupational census data (1881–1931)

concepts.name: Pre-Colonial Indian Textile Industry: Status and Global Significance
key_dimensions: India's share in global textile trade before 1757 (estimated 25% of world manufacturing output)
Key textile centres: Dhaka (muslin), Surat (silk/cotton), Murshidabad, Masulipatnam, Calicut
Nature of production: cottage/artisan-based vs. proto-industrial guild systems
Export commodities and trading routes through Mughal mercantile networks and European East India Companies

concepts.name: Differential Tariff Policy: Discriminatory Duties
key_dimensions: Indian textiles exported to Britain faced duties of 70–80%, while British cloth entered India at 2–3.5%
Contrast with mercantilist protection Britain offered to its own manufacturers (Calico Acts 1690, 1720)
R.C. Dutt's critique: systematic policy reversal after 1813 Charter Act (end of EIC monopoly)
UPSC trap: Difference between revenue tariffs (for income) vs. protective tariffs (for industry) — Britain imposed former, denied latter to India

concepts.name: The Calico Acts (1690 & 1720): Implications for Indian Trade
key_dimensions: British parliament banned import/use of Indian printed cotton to protect domestic woolen and silk industries
Paradox: Britain protected itself from Indian competition while later forcing open Indian markets
Role of EIC in lobbying against Calico Acts when its profits depended on Indian textile trade
Transition point: post-Industrial Revolution, Britain reversed stance and sought Indian markets for Manchester goods

concepts.name: Industrial Revolution in Britain and Its Asymmetric Impact on India
key_dimensions: Mechanized production in Lancashire and Manchester mills drastically reduced cost of British cloth
Timeline: Power loom (1785), spinning jenny, steam engine — cost advantage over Indian handloom weavers
India simultaneously became raw material supplier (raw cotton) and market for finished goods — classic colonial trap
UPSC trap: Industrial Revolution benefited Britain partly due to capital extracted from India (drain of wealth thesis connection)

concepts.name: Charter Act of 1813: End of EIC Monopoly and Free Trade Imposition
key_dimensions: Threw open Indian trade to all British merchants — flooded Indian markets with cheap British textiles
EIC's own interest in Indian textiles (as exporter) had previously provided some incidental protection
Free trade ideology used selectively: free for British imports into India, not for Indian exports to Britain
Connection to Manchester Lobby's political pressure on British Parliament

concepts.name: Dacca Muslin Industry: Case Study of Decline
key_dimensions: Dacca muslin (Woven Air/Dhaka muslin) — world-renowned luxury textile, exported to Rome, Persia, Europe
Decline factors: loss of Mughal court patronage, British tariff policy, competition from Manchester mill cloth
Apocryphal but symbolically significant narrative: thumbs of weavers cut off (debated by historians — used as metaphor for forced decline)
Census evidence: Dacca population fell from 150,000 to 30,000–50,000 between 1765 and 1840 (Buchanan Hamilton's surveys)
UPSC trap: Muslin decline is often conflated with general handloom decline — Dacca was a specialized luxury segment

concepts.name: Role of East India Company in Distorting Weaver Economics
key_dimensions: Gomastha system: EIC appointed agents who advanced loans (dadni) to weavers, binding them contractually
Weavers could not sell to other buyers once they accepted advances — monopsony exploitation
Piece-rate manipulation: EIC paid below-market prices, used coercive methods including imprisonment
Distinction from later colonial period: EIC era (pre-1858) involved direct production coercion; post-1858 was market-based displacement

concepts.name: Drain of Wealth Theory and Its Connection to Textile Decline
key_dimensions: Dadabhai Naoroji's 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901): linked textile decline to overall economic drain
Mechanism: India exported raw cotton, imported finished cloth — net value drain from Indian economy
R.C. Dutt's 'Economic History of India' (1902): calculated loss from de-industrialization of weavers
UPSC trap: Drain theory is broader than textile decline — textile de-industrialization is one component, not the whole theory

concepts.name: Railways and Their Dual Role: Market Integration vs. Industrial Displacement
key_dimensions: Railways (post-1853) penetrated interior markets, enabling cheap British cloth to reach previously protected hinterland weavers
Destroyed regional price differentials that had allowed local handloom industries to survive
Counter-argument: Railways also allowed Indian raw cotton and some textiles to reach ports more efficiently
UPSC trap: Railways are often presented as purely beneficial — examiners test whether students recognize the displacement effect on artisans

concepts.name: Swadeshi Movement (1905) as a Response to Textile De-industrialization
key_dimensions: Boycott of British cloth as direct nationalist response to destruction of Indian textile industry
Revival of handloom weaving as economic nationalism — connection between Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Aurobindo and textile boycott
Bengal partition (1905) as trigger, but underlying economic grievance rooted in decades of textile decline
Gandhi's Charkha (spinning wheel) as later evolution — philosophical and economic symbolism of reversing de-industrialization

concepts.name: Gandhi's Charkha and Khadi Movement: Economic vs. Symbolic Dimensions
key_dimensions: Charkha as instrument of economic self-sufficiency — direct challenge to Manchester cloth dependence
All India Spinners Association (1925) and All India Village Industries Association (1934) — institutional framework
Debate with Nehru and industrialists: Gandhi's village-economy model vs. large-scale industrialization approach
UPSC trap: Khadi movement was NOT merely symbolic — it had a concrete economic program for rural employment and import substitution

concepts.name: Indian Cotton Textile Mills: Emergence and Limited Compensation
key_dimensions: First cotton mill: Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company (1854) — Indian entrepreneurs responding to colonial conditions
Mills concentrated in Bombay and Ahmedabad — did NOT adequately compensate for handloom weaver displacement
Mills produced coarser counts of yarn/cloth; finer weaving remained with handlooms — market segmentation
British India government's countervailing excise duty (1894) on Indian mill cloth — even domestic industry taxed to protect Lancashire

concepts.name: Countervailing Excise Duty of 1894: Taxation of Indian Mill Industry
key_dimensions: When India imposed 5% import duty on foreign cloth (revenue purpose), Britain forced India to impose equal 5% excise on Indian mill cloth
Effectively neutralized any competitive advantage Indian mills might have gained from import duty
Exposed the fiction of 'free trade' — it was managed trade in Britain's favor
Removed only in 1925 after sustained nationalist pressure — timeline important for UPSC

concepts.name: Silk and Woolen Industries: Parallel Destruction Beyond Cotton
key_dimensions: Murshidabad silk industry decline: lost court patronage, competition from European silk (especially after Suez Canal 1869)
Kashmir shawl industry: decline due to Jacquard loom imitations of Kashmiri patterns made in Paisley, Scotland (Paisley shawl)
Woolen industries of Punjab and Rajasthan undercut by cheap imported woolen goods
UPSC trap: Textile de-industrialization is often reduced to cotton alone — silk and wool segments are tested in Mains

concepts.name: Occupational Displacement of Weavers: Social and Demographic Consequences
key_dimensions: Weavers forced into agriculture — 'destruction of urban artisan class' and 'ruralization of India' thesis
Census data (1881, 1901, 1911): declining proportion of population in manufacturing/artisan occupations
Emergence of rural poverty and indebtedness among displaced weavers — connection to peasant distress
Caste-based weaver communities (Julahas, Devanga, Koshti) — social disintegration alongside economic displacement

concepts.name: Raw Cotton Export Policy and Its Contradiction with Textile Decline
key_dimensions: India exported raw cotton to British mills while importing finished cloth — structural dependency
American Civil War (1861–65): cotton famine in Britain boosted Indian raw cotton exports temporarily — short-term gain, long-term trap
Farmers incentivized to grow cotton as cash crop → food crop displacement → vulnerability to famines
UPSC trap: Raw cotton export boom is sometimes presented as 'British development of India' — must be contextualized as extractive

concepts.name: Nationalist Economic Critique vs. Imperialist Justification of Textile Decline
key_dimensions: Nationalist view (Naoroji, Dutt, Gokhale): deliberate policy destruction for British industrial benefit
Imperialist/apologist view (John Strachey, some Cambridge historians): 'natural' outcome of industrial progress, India benefited from cheaper cloth
Morris D. Morris's revisionist argument: de-industrialization was not uniform; some regions and industries survived or adapted
UPSC examiner angle: Tests whether students can present both sides and offer a balanced, evidence-based conclusion

concepts.name: Fiscal Autonomy Denial and Its Role in Textile Industry Destruction
key_dimensions: India had no independent tariff policy — fiscal decisions made in London in British commercial interests
Government of India Act 1919 gave limited fiscal autonomy; full fiscal autonomy restored only in 1921 (Meston Award)
Indian Fiscal Commission (1921–22): recommended protective tariffs — first acknowledgment of legitimate industrial protection need
UPSC trap: Fiscal autonomy is often linked only to political history — its direct economic consequence for textile industry is a high-yield connection

concepts.name: Handloom Weaving Survival and Resilience: Nuancing the Decline Narrative
key_dimensions: Handloom sector did NOT completely disappear — survived in specialized niches (Banarasi silk, Kanjeevaram, Pochampalli, Chanderi)
Reasons for survival: unique designs, cultural significance, cost-competitiveness in fine weaving, domestic demand
Post-independence: All India Handloom Board (1952), Handloom Reservation Act (1985) — policy continuity from colonial grievances
UPSC trap: Overstatement of complete destruction is incorrect — nuanced answer acknowledging survival alongside displacement scores higher in Mains
